# Independent adversarial audit: half-integer symmetric chain localization


convex-compatibility hypotheses.** No repair to the theorem statement is
needed. The assertion that all positive-depth globally maximizing bases
are 0 or 1 is justified by the cited strict one-integer-coordinate theorem,
not merely by symmetry or ordinary quasiconcavity.

I read the complete following notes, including their proofs:

- `candidate 5e6e53a58ea7a59b`
- `candidate 9afb6a8708a420d7`
- `candidate 44a12d13f3aabab3`
- `candidate 96f963f75f5ed816`

I also checked their archived independent audits. This audit independently
checks the actual applicability conditions rather than treating those
previous verdicts as a substitute for the argument.

## 1. Existence and positive depth

Positive-volume fibers of a one-integer-coordinate convex source form a
finite consecutive integer interval. Minkowski interpolation between any
two positive fibers gives positive volume at every intervening integer.
Half-integer reflection sends that interval to itself and exchanges the
indices 0 and 1. A nonempty such positive interval necessarily contains
both 0 and 1.

In every positive fiber, a point with an interior ball has positive mixed
depth: every nonvertical containing halfspace captures at least half that
ball, while a vertical containing halfspace captures its entire own fiber.
The depth function on each bounded fiber is continuous by the uniform
slab bound after normalizing the continuous normal. Equivalently, the
n=1 finite-tilt clipping argument proves compact attainment of the cap
minimum. There are finitely many compact candidate fibers, so the global
maximum exists and is positive.

A zero-d-volume fiber lies strictly outside the positive integer interval.
The outward vertical closed tail at that index excludes all positive
fibers and therefore has zero mixed d-volume. Such a candidate cannot
attain the positive global maximum. This uses the one-dimensional base
order and the specified d-volume measure; it is not a claim about an
arbitrary lower-dimensional intrinsic-measure problem.

## 2. The strict interpolation dependency really applies

The strict theorem assumes precisely a compact convex source in R×R^d,
finite positive total mixed d-volume, and two positive-depth points at
distinct integer bases. It imposes no facet-free, smoothness, or
non-supporting-section hypothesis. I checked its treatment of supporting
sections, which is the potential issue exposed by the plateau archive:

1. Positive depth forces an interior point of its own positive fiber,
   using a supporting affine majorant of the concave fiber support roof.
2. An attaining nonvertical cap exists at an intermediate integer point
   by finite tilt clipping. If interpolation had exactly the endpoint
   depth, this cap would have to pass through both endpoints; otherwise
   moving it to the strictly contained endpoint removes a positive slab.
3. In the one-dimensional base order, all positive sections strictly
   inside the real section-projection interval are proper cuts. Only the
   two extreme section indices can be supporting cuts.
4. Their section volumes form a log-concave sequence (constant one in
   the d=1, zero-dimensional-section case). At a supporting endpoint the
   one-sided derivative allows its weight to be decreased between zero
   and its full value; all proper interior weights remain compulsory.
5. Integer-tilt stationarity at each endpoint puts its integer coordinate
   in the centroid interval obtained by trimming those two endpoint
   weights. Log-concavity bounds that interval's length by one. Thus two
   equal-depth endpoints separated by at least two integer steps cannot
   both minimize the same intermediate cap.

Every hypothesis is met for a reflected pair of global maximizers
(j,x) and (1−j,x). If j∉{0,1}, their base separation is at least three.
Either 0 or 1 is a strictly intermediate integer, and the convex
combination with that base has continuous coordinate exactly x. Convexity
places it in the actual corresponding fiber; positive-depth endpoints
also place it in that fiber's interior. The strict theorem then gives
larger depth, contradicting global maximality.

Therefore every globally maximizing base is 0 or 1. Reflection ensures
that at least one maximizing point occurs at each of these two bases.
The statement does not say every point of either fiber is maximizing.

## 3. Why the unbounded-maximizing-base archive does not contradict this

The archived plateau family has TWO integer coordinates (p,q). Its many
maximizers are at bases (j,0), but the q-coordinate remains discrete and
contributes distinct measured fibers. Treating q as a continuous fiber
coordinate would change counting×Lebesgue measure into ordinary Lebesgue
measure and would not preserve the depth problem.

Equivalently, after aggregating across q, the section weights indexed by
p need not satisfy the log-concavity and two-optional-endpoint property
used in §2. That is exactly the applicability boundary stated by the
strict n=1 theorem. Neither a planar arrangement of some maximizing bases
nor their having the same q-coordinate reduces the integer dimension of
the whole source. Thus no archived plateau meets the hypotheses used in
the present localization proof.

## 4. Movable diagonal and permitted transformations

For common-vertex simplex fibers r_jT_d, permutations of continuous
coordinates are genuine ambient measure-preserving source symmetries.
Averaging a maximizing point over them stays in its convex own fiber and
cannot decrease depth, because depth superlevel sets are convex. This
produces a maximizing diagonal point (0,t·1), initially with
0≤t≤R/d.

The touching majorant is r_j≤R with slope zero, since the two central
radii are maximal. The cited movable-diagonal theorem is applicable:
on the upper diagonal segment t≥R/(d+1), original depth equals the
positive-normal restricted depth, which is nonincreasing in t. Thus a
maximizer there may be replaced by the own centroid endpoint. The common
vertex t=0 has zero depth, since the closed cap X_1≤0 captures zero
d-volume in every original fiber. Consequently a maximizer may be chosen
with exactly the stated range

    0<t≤R/(d+1).

This is an existence statement for a chosen maximizer, not a claim that
all maximizing points have that range. It does not assert that the own
centroid is always optimal.

The base reflection z↦1−z is an integer translation followed by sign
reversal and preserves the original integer lattice. Continuous-coordinate
permutations preserve every fiber volume. The fiberwise vertex swaps used
inside the cited comparison are not claimed to be ambient symmetries;
their exact cap comparison retains its majorant and tied roof term. No
untracked affine lattice transformation occurs.

## 5. Tilt sign, boundaries, and the large-tilt estimate

For a cap with positive integer tilt b at base 0, the two members of pair
{−h,h+1} have thresholds bh and −b(h+1). For tilt −b the thresholds are
−bh and b(h+1). Subtracting the latter pair mass from the former gives

    [F_h(−b(h+1))−F_h(−bh)]
     +[F_h(bh)−F_h(b(h+1))]≥0.

Both signs are correct. Closed-tail monotonicity proves the inequality
even at atoms or supporting boundaries. Hence minimizing over all tilts
can indeed be restricted to nonpositive tilt at base 0, with the reversed
sign at base 1. There remains ONE shared tilt for the entire original
source.

At the own centroid, the positive-normal reduction uses r_j≤R and is
valid. Normalize w≥0 by Σw_i=1. In the cap

    −βz+w·X≥t,     t=R/(d+1), β≥t,

every left outer fiber z=−h, h≥1, has nonpositive continuous threshold
and is entirely captured, including equality. The central fiber supplies
at least γ_d R^d V_d. Their combined payment is

    V_d[γ_dR^d+Σ_(h≥1)r_h^d]≥γ_dV_dΣ_(h≥0)r_h^d,

which is exactly the desired absolute n=1 OC payment. All other fibers
contribute nonnegative mass. A vertical through-base-0 cap captures at
least one entire member of every pair and hence at least half the total
mass; its full boundary fiber is retained. Zero-radius terminal fibers
have zero d-volume and do not change these conclusions.

The remaining parameter set 0≤β<t is therefore stated correctly. The
note does not claim that its depth bound has been proved, and correctly
warns that a movable point below the own centroid retains a nonzero tied
roof penalty. No unresolved small-tilt sector is hidden by the reductions.
